## VOICES

![Pedro Salmerón Sanginés](https://mexicosolidarity.com/wp-
content/uploads/2026/09/salmeron-01.jpg)

    
    
    Pedro Salmerón Sanginés holds a doctorate in history from the National Autonomous University of Mexico (UNAM) and has written 17 books and 50 articles. He’s an independent journalist and lifelong leftist activist

**What kind of revolutionary activities were going on before 1810? Were women
involved?**

![The allegorical figure representing Independence \(center\) flanked by
Miguel Hidalgo \(left\) and General Agustín Iturbide
](https://mexicosolidarity.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/salmeron-02.jpg)The
allegorical figure representing Independence (center) flanked by Miguel
Hidalgo (left) and General Agustín Iturbide (right). Anonymous, Allegory of
Independence, 1834 (Museo Histórico Curato de Dolores, Guanajato, INAH)

I don’t know if you could call it “revolutionary,” but there were a ton of
agrarian revolts—without a political program—in 18th-century “New Spain.” They
were community-based rebellions, so of course women participated.

![In many areas, as much as 90% of the native population died off between the
start of the Conquista in 1519 and the begin](https://mexicosolidarity.com/wp-
content/uploads/2026/09/salmeron-03.jpg)In many areas, as much as 90% of the
native population died off between the start of the Conquista in 1519 and the
beginning of the 18th Century.

But in terms of political revolution, those were mostly conspiratorial groups
made up of middle-class criollos and mixed-race descendants of Spaniards, some
holding government positions. Those who start revolutions are never slaves or
those dying of hunger; they have no time to even think about revolution! Why
at that time? Napoleon Bonaparte had invaded Spain and imposed his son as the
Spanish king; Spain was in chaos, and that provided opportunities for the
colonies. In 1810, one conspirator playing a pivotal role was Doña Josefa
Ortíz Tellez Girón, the wife of a town mayor in the state of Querétaro. The
conspiracy was discovered, and she sent the warning message to fellow
conspirators in Guanajuato.

![Josefa Ortiz Téllez Girón](https://mexicosolidarity.com/wp-
content/uploads/2026/09/salmeron-04.jpg)Josefa Ortiz Téllez Girón

**Why did the Revolution begin in Guanajuato?**

Hearing the warning, most Guanajuato conspirators wanted to flee. But not the
parish priest Miguel Hidalgo! He was no bumpkin. He was cultured, read banned
books, translated Moliere from the French and directed theater. He said, “We
can’t get anywhere—where would we run to? What we have to do is capture the
Spaniards and take over the village!”

So they captured some Spaniards, released people from prison and burned the
archives—the official records of who owns and who owes what, who has a prison
record, and all kinds of possibly harmful information.

After securing the town, he rang the alarm bell and called the people to mass;
it was Sunday, a market day with large crowds. With his Grito de Dolores, his
famous “cry” or “call to action from the town of Dolores,” he told the people
to start a revolution.

In only twelve days, the rebellion spread to all the towns of the region whose
inhabitants were workers on the haciendas and in the mines; these were not
indigenous people, by the way. Not just men, but entire families rose up. Like
the nomads of Mongolia, they all moved together. Women participated directly
in this event.

![In the first years, New Spain was marked by tensions and outbreaks that
questioned the solidity of viceregal authority.
](https://mexicosolidarity.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/salmeron-05.jpg)In
the first years, New Spain was marked by tensions and outbreaks that
questioned the solidity of viceregal authority. Indigenous rebellions, Creole
conspiracies, lawsuits between authorities and popular riots showed that the
Castilian administration had to invest as much effort in preserving its
dominion as in acquiring it. Photo courtesy of Xikoova.com.

The workers and peasants demanded an end to slavery and an end to paying
tributes to the crown; Hidalgo took up their demands, which went beyond those
of the original criollo conspirators.

**Did women participate actively in Mexico’s War of Independence?**

Middle-class criollo women played one role—they formed support networks and
carried out espionage, propaganda and journalism. Josefa Ortíz is a good
example.

![Servante Indienne \[Indian Woman Servant\] by Claudio Linati,
1830](https://mexicosolidarity.com/wp-
content/uploads/2026/09/salmeron-06.jpg)Servante Indienne [Indian Woman
Servant] by Claudio Linati, 1830

The village women played the other main role. They fed the guerillas by
growing food and tending livestock—the usual economy had come to a stop.

An example: With María José Garrido, I researched the court records of
Pénjamo, Guanajuato. In November 1814, about 300 women and their children were
arrested and incarcerated in convents, without cause. Why were they locked up?
Spanish Colonel Agustín de Iturbide wanted to stop the women from providing
the rebels with food and other necessities in order to, as Mao said, “take
away the water from the fish.” He proposed burning six villages of insurgents
and shooting 50 of the women.

The viceroy told him not to shoot women, but the colonel declared, “In my
view, women of this sort cause greater harm than men who band together;
regardless of arguments citing laws designed to protect this sex—which, while
deserving of consideration regarding its inherent frailty … cannot simply be
left free to perpetrate wrongs of such gravity and consequence—one need only
consider the power the fair sex holds over a man’s heart to understand the
harm they are causing.”

![Pénjamo, Guanajuato. Although their names are not in the books of the
history of Mexico, Penjamo women supporters of
the](https://mexicosolidarity.com/wp-
content/uploads/2026/09/salmeron-07.jpg)Pénjamo, Guanajuato. Although their
names are not in the books of the history of Mexico, Penjamo women supporters
of the revolt were imprisoned in 1814.

The women were finally released in 1817 for lack of evidence; María Regina
Barrón, a woman leader of Pénjamo, argued their case before the judges. Across
the southern mountains, in Bajío, Oaxaca and Veracruz, the same support from
women was continuing—the guerrilla forces relied on women for logistics; women
were the backbone.

Colonel Iturbide also arrested Tomasa Esteves and five other women who had
seduced Royalist forces and convinced them to switch sides. The women were
labeled prostitutes in the documents, negating their political role, and
incarcerated in convents in Guanajuato. But they weren’t the only women who
used sex as a tool in service to the revolution.

**Did women see the revolution as an opportunity for women to gain greater
freedom?**

Not directly. However, indirectly, when the revolution dismantled the old
economy based on plantations and mining, women finally escaped their virtual
slavery as the wives of slaves. Feudal labor relations ended, and although
they weren’t explicitly fighting for it, women subsequently began putting
forward their own demands in the 30s and 40s—the right to own property, to
inherit and to divorce.

![On the high plateau of central México at nearly 7000 feet is the city of
Guanajuato, originally named Real de Minas de
G](https://mexicosolidarity.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/salmeron-08.jpg)On
the high plateau of central México at nearly 7000 feet is the city of
Guanajuato, originally named Real de Minas de Guanajuato (Royal Mines of
Guanajuato). It was founded in 1548 by colonial Spain for one reason only: to
make Spain rich. Silver and gold extraction were foundational to Spain’s
political economy, and in those times the mines of Guanajuato were the most
productive in México. Photo courtesy of the Mexico Solidarity Project.

**Can you tell the story of a woman who was particularly important?**

Leona Vicario, born in 1789, was educated and attractive; she wrote and played
the piano. She formed a secret group called Los Guadalupes—the Virgin of
Guadalupe was the emblem of the resistance—that raised funds for the rebel
army of José María Morelos. In 1813, she was arrested and put into a convent.
All the funds she managed were confiscated. But, dressed as a man, she made a
spectacular escape down a rope made from bedsheets and joined up with
Morelos’s army. She had no other place else to go. She married Andres Quintana
Roo during this time. Did she find another way to contribute? She wrote—she
was the first wartime correspondent in the country!

She had her first baby in 1817 in a cave while fleeing the enemy army but was
caught and incarcerated again. It was only through Quintana Roo’s negotiations
that she was freed.

After the war ended, she was set to retire. But the newspapers began claiming
that women played no part in the revolution, that Josefa Ortiz couldn’t even
read or write, and that she herself was involved merely out of love. Leona
Vicario responded in print to the conservative leader Lucas Alamán. She said,
“You believe—as men do—that we women act solely out of instinct and passion.
You do not know us, and you know nothing of our ideas.” And with that, she
returned to politics! At her death in 1842, she was the first woman who
received a full state funeral. They called her the “Beloved Mother of the
Country.”

![Women continue to fight for Mexico! Diego Rivera, The Uprising, 1931.
Collection of Marcos and Vicky Micha Levy. © 2019
](https://mexicosolidarity.com/wp-
content/uploads/2026/09/salmeron-09.jpg)Women continue to fight for Mexico!
Diego Rivera, The Uprising, 1931. Collection of Marcos and Vicky Micha Levy. ©
2019 Banco de México Diego Rivera Frida Kahlo Museums Trust, Mexico, D.F. /
Artists Rights Society (ARS), New York

AMLO named 2020 the year of Leona Vicario, 2019 the year of Zapata, and 2023
the year of Villa—he put her on the same level.

**Does Claudia Sheinbaum come from the lineage of revolutionary women?**

Every Thursday, at the mañanera, she includes a historical capsule about a
woman teacher, nurse, soldier or journalist—a woman whose story is not
commonly known but should be. Like Leona Vicario, she insists on the capacity
of women and for us to recognize their contributions.

![Statue of Leona Vicario, Chetumal](https://mexicosolidarity.com/wp-
content/uploads/2026/09/salmeron-10.jpg)Statue of Leona Vicario, Chetumal

Chetumal, the capital of Quintana Roo, a state named for Leona Vicario’s
husband, erected a statue of her. Engraved in the stone it says, “I am Leona,
and I want to live like a wild beast.” Leona is Spanish for lion. I think that
could apply to our ferocious Claudia too.
